newsitem.title: USA: Balloonist thwarted by Libya, round-world bid dims.
newsitem.headline: Balloonist thwarted by Libya, round-world bid dims.

text.p: American balloonist Steve Fossett was denied permission to fly over Libya on Friday, forcing a detour that could prevent him from becoming the first person to circle the globe nonstop in a balloon.
But Fossett, 52, refused to give up, telling his control centre in Chicago he wanted to "go for it."
At 4:30 p.m. EST (2130 GMT) he was drifting southeasterly over Algeria at a comparatively slow 38 knots, expected to cross into Niger around 8 p.m. EST (0100 GMT Saturday).
He was at 18,500 feet (5,639 metres) and had been told to maintain an altitude of at least 10,000 feet (3,048 metres) over Chad and Niger because of unrest in those countries.

Project manager Bo Kemper said India looked like the most logical end point for the journey, if weather conditions stall Fossett's progress. If he winds up there he would have made it roughly half way around the world.
"The team and Steve are very disappointed," Kemper told reporters.
"But on the other hand it has been an unbelievably successful trip. Equipment worked 100 percent. The weather was working 100 percent. The only thing that didn't work was political," he said.

The political news came in a three-line telegram from the Libyan government with a terse denial signed "best regards." It ended days of back-channel and public negotiating to win permission for Fossett to use Libyan airspace.

The new route, over Egypt after Niger and Chad, will cause Fossett to use an extra day-and-a-half's worth of fuel, Kemper said. More importantly, he said, the dip south would take him out of the favourable wind current that pushed him across the Atlantic in three days.
"It's like the train is leaving the station without him," Kemper said. "The chances of him recovering (the winds) are negligible."
"It doesn't look good," he added. "It significantly reduces our chances."
The U.S. State Department condemned Libya's refusal to let Fossett cross the country, saying it reflected the "paranoia of the Libyan leadership."
While Kemper refused to call the mission over, he said "The only reason to keep flying will be to break the duration record."
The current mark for time spent in a balloon is six days and 16 minutes set in 1981 by Richard Abruzzo and Troy Bradley. Fossett's trip began late on Monday in St. Louis.

He got the bad news from Libya just after breaking his own record for balloon distance travel when he passed 5,435 miles (8,747 km) over Algeria. Kemper set the earlier mark on a voyage from South Korea to Canada.

Fossett was cold and needed sleep, Kemper said. The Algerian government required him to call air traffic controllers every 30 minutes, which kept him awake. A chase plane sent by the expedition was trying to help with some of the check-ins so he could sleep.
The Colorado-based Fossett, who made his fortune in the Chicago futures markets, was eating military rations, including rice and chicken that can be heated. His bathroom is a bucket.

Kemper said that rival ballonists Richard Branson and Jean Piccard, who tried and failed in separate missions this month to capture the record Fossett sought, had both attempted to intercede with Libya on Fossett's behalf.
He said British tycoon Branson had permission to cross Libya had his flight been successful.
Kemper said the expedition hoped Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi would see reports on the balloon on CNN and act to let Fossett cross.
"My guess is that Col. Gaddafi knew what was going on," Kemper said.
Libya's hostile relations with the United States left the two countries without formal diplomatic ties.
